The owner of Profitacre executed an instrument in the proper form of a deed, purporting to convey Profitacre "to my brother for life, then to my nephew in fee simple." The brother, who is the owner's brother and nephew's father, promptly began to manage Profitacre, which is valuable income-producing real estate. The brother collected all rents and paid all expenses, including real estate taxes. The nephew did not object, and this state of affairs continued for five years until 1987. In that year, the brother executed an instrument in the proper form of a deed, purporting to convey Profitacre to his girlfriend. The nephew, no admirer of the girlfriend, asserted his right to ownership of Profitacre. The girlfriend asserted her ownership and said that if the nephew had any rights he was obligated to pay real estate taxes, even though the brother had been kind enough to pay them in the past. Income from Profitacre is ample to cover expenses, including real estate taxes. In an appropriate action to determine the rights of the parties, the court should decide

Choices:
A. The brother's purported deed forfeited his life estate, so the nephew owns Profitacre in fee simple.
B. The girlfriend owns an estate for her life, is entitled to all income, and must pay real estate taxes; the nephew owns the remainder interest.
C. The girlfriend owns an estate for the life of the brother, is entitled to all income, and must pay real estate taxes; the nephew owns the remainder interest.
D. The girlfriend owns an estate for the life of the brother and is entitled to all income; the nephew owns the remainder interest, and must pay real estate taxes.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Estates in land, specifically life estates and vested remainders, and the rights and responsibilities associated with each.

Fact Analysis: The owner of Profitacre conveyed the property to the brother for life, with a vested remainder in the nephew. The brother managed the property, collected rents, and paid expenses, including real estate taxes, for five years before conveying the property to his girlfriend. The nephew asserts his right to ownership, while the girlfriend claims ownership and suggests the nephew is responsible for paying real estate taxes.

Rule Application: A life tenant has the right to convey their interest, but the conveyance is only valid for the duration of the measuring life. The life tenant also has a duty not to commit voluntary or permissive waste, which includes paying real estate taxes. A vested remainder is unaffected by the life tenant's conveyance. In this case, the brother's conveyance to the girlfriend created a life estate in the girlfriend, lasting for the remainder of the brother's life, with the nephew retaining the vested remainder.

Legal Conclusion: The girlfriend owns a life estate for the duration of the brother's life, is entitled to all income, and must pay real estate taxes to avoid committing permissive waste. The nephew owns the vested remainder interest, which is unaffected by the brother's conveyance to the girlfriend. Therefore, the correct answer is C.

A woman owned Blackacre, her home. Her daughter lived with her and always referred to Blackacre as "my property." Two years ago, the daughter, for a valuable consideration, executed and delivered to her boyfriend an instrument in the proper form of a warranty deed purporting to convey Blackacre to the boyfriend in fee simple, reserving to herself an estate for two years in Blackacre. The boyfriend promptly and properly recorded the deed. One year ago, the woman died and by will, duly admitted to probate, left her entire estate to the daughter. One month ago, the daughter, for a valuable consideration, executed and delivered to a buyer an instrument in the proper form of a warranty deed purporting to convey Blackacre to the buyer, who promptly and properly recorded the deed. The daughter was then in possession of Blackacre and the buyer had no actual knowledge of the deed to the boyfriend. Immediately thereafter, the daughter gave possession to the buyer. The recording act of the jurisdiction provides: "No conveyance or mortgage of real property shall be good against subsequent purchasers for value and without notice unless the same be recorded according to law." Last week, the daughter fled the jurisdiction. Upon learning the facts, the buyer brought an appropriate action against the boyfriend to quiet title to Blackacre. If the buyer wins, it will be because

Choices:
A. the daughter had nothing to convey to the boyfriend two years ago.
B. the daughter's deed to the boyfriend was not to take effect until after the daughter's deed to the buyer.
C. the buyer was first in possession.
D. the daughter's deed to the boyfriend was not in the buyer's chain of title.

Answer: D

Fact Analysis: The daughter executed a warranty deed to the boyfriend two years ago, reserving an estate for two years, and the boyfriend recorded the deed. The buyer had no notice of the earlier deed because it was not in their chain of title.

Rule Application: Under a notice act, a bona fide purchaser who records their deed without notice of earlier purchasers will prevail. To be a bona fide purchaser, one must give value for their interest in the land and record without notice. The buyer meets these requirements, having given value and recorded without notice of the boyfriend's deed, which was not in their chain of title.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the buyer recorded without notice of earlier purchasers and is protected by the recording act, a judgment in their favor would be based on their status as a bona fide purchaser under the notice act, supporting option D.

A man died testate. The man's estate consisted of a residence as well as significant personal property. By his duly probated will, the man devised the residence to a friend who was specifically identified in the will. The residue of the estate was given to a stated charity. The value of the residence has increased significantly because of recent zoning changes. There is credible extrinsic evidence that the man wanted his friend to own the residence after the man's death so that the friend and his wife could care for their child there. There is no applicable statute. If both the charity and the child claim the residence, to whom should the estate distribute the residence?

A mother owned Blackacre, a two-family apartment house on a small city lot not suitable for partition-in-kind. Upon the mother's death, her will devised Blackacre to "my son and daughter." A week ago, a creditor obtained a money judgment against the son, and properly filed the judgment in the county where Blackacre is located. The son needed cash, but the daughter did not wish to sell Blackacre. The son commenced a partition action against the daughter and the creditor. Assume that the court properly ordered a partition by judicial sale. After the sale, the creditor's judgment will be a lien on

B. only a one-half interest in Blackacre.
C. all of the proceeds of a sale of Blackacre.
D. only the portion of the proceeds of sale due to the brother.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Partition of co-owned property, specifically the effect of a creditor's lien on a tenant in common's interest in real property.

Fact Analysis: The mother's will devised Blackacre to her son and daughter without indicating a clear intent to create a joint tenancy, resulting in them owning the property as tenants in common with equal 50% interests. A creditor obtained a judgment against the son and filed it in the county where Blackacre is located, creating a lien on the son's interest in the property.

Rule Application: A creditor's lien only attaches to the interest in the property owned by the debtor, in this case, the son's 50% interest in Blackacre as a tenant in common. At that time, Blackacre was owned by the man's father; the man had no title to Blackacre and was not the agent of the father. D. judgment for specific performance, to prevent unjust enrichment of the man.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Specific performance in contract law, particularly the enforceability of a contract when the seller acquires title to the property after the contract's execution but before the closing date.

Fact Analysis: The man entered into a valid written contract to sell Blackacre to the purchaser, despite having no title to the property at the time. Rule Application: In contract law, a seller's acquisition of title to the property after the contract's execution but before the closing date can render the contract enforceable. An owner owned 80 acres of land, fronting on a town road. Two years ago, the owner sold to a buyer the back 40 acres. The 40 acres sold to the buyer did not adjoin any public road. The owner's deed to the buyer expressly granted a right-of-way over a specified strip of the owner's retained 40 acres, so the buyer could reach the town road. The deed was promptly and properly recorded. Last year, the buyer conveyed the back 40 acres to a doctor. They had discussed the right-of-way over the owner's land to the road, but the buyer's deed to the doctor made no mention of it. The doctor began to use the right-of-way as the buyer had, but the owner sued to enjoin such use by the doctor. The court should decide for

Choices:
A. the doctor, because he has an easement by implication.
B. the doctor, because the easement appurtenant passed to him as a result of the buyer's deed to him.
C. the owner, because the buyer's easement in gross was not transferable.
D. the owner, because the buyer's deed failed expressly to transfer the right-of-way to the doctor.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Easements in property law, specifically the distinction between easements appurtenant and easements in gross, and how they are transferred with land.

Fact Analysis: The owner sold 40 acres to the buyer with an express grant of a right-of-way over the owner's retained land for access to the town road. The buyer then sold the land to the doctor without mentioning the right-of-way in the deed. The doctor continued to use the right-of-way as the buyer had.

Rule Application: An easement appurtenant, which benefits a specific piece of land, automatically runs with the land and does not need to be re-identified in subsequent deeds after initial recording. This contrasts with an easement in gross, which is a personal right and not transferable without express grant.

Legal Conclusion: Since the easement in question is an easement appurtenant and was properly recorded, it would automatically pass to the doctor with the land, regardless of its omission in the buyer's deed to the doctor. Therefore, the correct decision is in favor of the doctor, supporting option B.

A farmer and a rancher owned Greenacre, a large farm, in fee simple as tenants in common, each owning an undivided one-half interest. For five years the farmer occupied Greenacre and conducted farming operations. The farmer never accounted to the rancher for any income, but the farmer did pay all real estate taxes when the taxes were due and kept the buildings located on Greenacre insured against loss from fire, storm, and flood. The rancher lived in a distant city and was interested only in realizing a profit from the sale of the land when market conditions produced the price the rancher wanted. The farmer died intestate, survived only by the farmer's sole heir. Thereafter, the sole heir occupied Greenacre but was inexperienced in farming operations. The result was a financial disaster. The sole heir failed to pay real estate taxes for two years. The appropriate governmental authority held a tax sale to recover the taxes due. At such sale the rancher was the only bidder and obtained a conveyance from the appropriate governmental authority upon payment of an amount sufficient to discharge the amounts due for taxes, plus interest and penalties, and the costs of holding the tax sale. The amount paid was one-third of the reasonable market value of Greenacre. Thereafter, the rancher instituted an appropriate action against the sole heir to quiet title in and to recover possession of Greenacre. The sole heir asserted all defenses available to her. Except for the statutes related to real estate taxes and tax sales, there is no applicable statute. In this lawsuit, the rancher is entitled to a decree quieting title so that the rancher is the sole owner in fee simple of Greenacre

Choices:
A. because the rancher survived the farmer.
B. because the farmer's sole heir defaulted in the obligations undertaken by the farmer.
C. unless the farmer's sole heir pays the rancher one-half of the reasonable market value of Greenacre.
D. unless the farmer's sole heir pays the rancher one-half of the amount the rancher paid for the tax deed.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Rights and duties of tenants in common, specifically the right to contribution for certain expenditures.

Fact Analysis: The farmer and the rancher owned Greenacre as tenants in common, each with an undivided one-half interest. The farmer paid all real estate taxes and kept the buildings insured, but never accounted to the rancher for any income. After the farmer's death, the sole heir failed to pay real estate taxes for two years, leading to a tax sale where the rancher obtained a conveyance for one-third of the reasonable market value of Greenacre.

Rule Application: Co-tenants have a right to contribution from each other for certain expenditures such as taxes. Since the farmer's sole heir failed to pay the taxes, she is responsible for contributing to the cost of the tax deed obtained by the rancher. An accounting is not necessary in this case as there is only one expenditure to divide.

Legal Conclusion: The rancher is entitled to a decree quieting title unless the farmer's sole heir pays the rancher one-half of the amount the rancher paid for the tax deed, which is the correct contribution for the tax expenditure.

The contract stipulated that the landowner would deliver to the purchaser, upon the payment of the last installment due, "a warranty deed sufficient to convey the fee simple." The contract contained no other provision that could be construed as referring to title. The purchaser entered into possession of Greenacre. After making 10 of the 300 installment payments obligated under the contract, the purchaser discovered that there was outstanding a valid and enforceable mortgage on Greenacre, securing the payment of debt in the amount of 25% of the purchase price the purchaser had agreed to pay. There was no evidence that the landowner had ever been late in payments due under the mortgage and there was no evidence of any danger of insolvency of the landowner. The value of Greenacre now is four times the amount on the debt secured by the mortgage. The purchaser quit possession of Greenacre and demanded that the landowner repay the amounts the purchaser had paid under the contract. After the landowner refused the demand, the purchaser brought an appropriate action against the landowner to recover damages for the landowner's alleged breach of the contract. In such action, should damages be awarded to the purchaser?

Legal Concept: The requirement of marketable title in real estate transactions, specifically in the context of installment purchase contracts.

Fact Analysis: The landowner and purchaser entered into a valid written installment purchase agreement for Greenacre, with the landowner to deliver a warranty deed upon the purchaser's payment of the last installment. The purchaser took possession and made 10 payments before discovering a valid mortgage on the property, then quit possession and demanded repayment.

Rule Application: In real estate transactions, including installment contracts, the seller is not required to provide marketable title until the closing date or the time for delivery of the deed. The obligation to provide marketable title is implied unless otherwise agreed upon, but the time for performance has not yet arrived if the closing date or final payment has not occurred.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the landowner's time for performance regarding marketable title has not yet arrived, as there are still 290 payments to be made under the installment contract, damages should not be awarded to the purchaser at this time, supporting option A.

A seller owned a single family house. A buyer gave the seller a signed handwritten offer to purchase the house. The offer was unconditional and sufficient to satisfy the statute of frauds, and when the seller signed an acceptance an enforceable contract resulted. The house on the land had been the seller's home, but he had moved to an apartment, so the house was vacant at all times relevant to the proposed transaction. Two weeks after the parties had entered into their contract, one week after the buyer had obtained a written mortgage lending commitment from a lender, and one week before the agreed-upon closing date, the house was struck by lightning and burned to the ground. The loss was not insured, because three years earlier, the seller had let his homeowner's insurance policy lapse after he had paid his mortgage debt in full. The handwritten contract was wholly silent as to matters of financing, risk of loss, and insurance. The buyer declared the contract voided by the fire, but the seller asserted a right to enforce the contract despite the loss. There is no applicable statute. If a court finds for the seller, what is the likely reason?

Choices:
A. The contract was construed against the buyer, who drafted it.
B. The lender's written commitment to make a mortgage loan to the buyer made the contract of sale fully binding on the buyer.
C. The risk of loss falls on the party in possession, and constructive possession passed to the buyer on the contract date.
D. The risk of loss passed to the buyer on the contract date under the doctrine of equitable conversion.

Legal Concept: The doctrine of equitable conversion in real estate transactions, particularly how it affects the risk of loss when a contract is silent on the matter.

The contract was unconditional and met the statute of frauds, resulting in an enforceable contract upon the seller's acceptance.

Rule Application: Under the doctrine of equitable conversion, the risk of loss passes to the party with the equitable title if the contract is silent. Equitable conversion occurs when the contract is capable of specific performance, which was the case here since the contract was unconditional and met the statute of frauds. Therefore, the risk of loss passed to the buyer, who had the equitable title at the time of the loss.

A landlord and a tenant orally agreed to a commercial tenancy for a term of six months beginning on July 1. Rent was to be paid by the first day of each month, and the tenant paid the first month's rent at the time of the agreement. When the tenant arrived at the leased premises on July 1, the tenant learned that the previous tenant had not vacated the premises at the end of her lease term on May 31 and did not intend to vacate. The tenant then successfully sued the previous tenant for possession. The tenant did not inform the landlord of the eviction action until after the tenant received possession. The tenant then sued the landlord, claiming damages for that portion of the lease period during which the tenant was not in possession. If the court finds for the landlord, what will be the most likely explanation?

Choices:
A. By suing the previous tenant for possession, the tenant elected that remedy in lieu of a suit against the landlord.
B. The landlord had delivered the legal right of possession to the tenant.
C. The tenant failed to timely vacate as required to sue for constructive eviction.
D. The tenant had not notified the landlord before bringing the eviction action.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Landlord's obligation to deliver possession of leased premises to a tenant, specifically the distinction between legal right of possession and actual possession.

Fact Analysis: The landlord and tenant entered into an oral agreement for a six-month commercial tenancy starting July 1, with the tenant paying the first month's rent upfront. However, upon arrival, the tenant found the previous tenant had not vacated, prompting the tenant to sue the previous tenant for possession without informing the landlord until after gaining possession.

Rule Application: A landlord is considered to have delivered the legal right of possession to a tenant if neither the landlord nor anyone holding of the landlord prevents the tenant from taking possession at the lease's commencement. In this case, the previous tenant's lease had ended, making them a trespasser not holding of the landlord, and thus the landlord had granted the legal right of possession to the tenant.

Legal Conclusion: Since the landlord had delivered the legal right of possession to the tenant, and there was no requirement in this jurisdiction for the landlord to also ensure actual possession, the court's finding for the landlord is justified, supporting option B.

An owner owned in fee simple three adjoining vacant lots fronting on a common street in a primarily residential section of a city which had no zoning laws. The lots were identified as Lots 1, 2, and 3. The owner conveyed Lot 1 to a man and Lot 2 to a woman. The owner retained Lot 3, which consisted of three acres of woodland. The woman, whose lot was between the other two, built a house on her lot. The woman's house included a large window on the side facing Lot 3. The window provided a beautiful view from her living room, thereby adding value to the woman's house. The man erected a house on his lot. The owner made no complaint to either the man or woman concerning the houses they built. After both the man and woman had completed their houses, the two of them agreed to and did build a common driveway running from the street to the rear of their respective lots. The driveway was built on the line between the two houses so that one-half of the way was located on each lot. The man and woman exchanged right-of-way deeds by which each of them conveyed to the other, his heirs and assigns, an easement to continue the right of way. Both deeds were properly recorded. After the man and woman had lived in their respective houses for thirty years, a new public street was built bordering on the rear of Lots 1, 2, and 3. The man informed the woman that, since the new street removed the need for their common driveway, he considered the right-of-way terminated; therefore, he intended to discontinue its use and expected the woman to do the same. At about the same time, the owner began the erection of a six-story apartment house on Lot 3. If the apartment house is completed, it will block the view from the woman's window and will substantially reduce the value of her lot. In an action brought by the woman to enjoin the owner from erecting the apartment building in such a way as to obstruct the view from the woman's living room window, the decision should be for

Choices:
A. the woman, because the owner's proposed building would be an obstruction of the woman's natural right to an easement for light and air.
B. the woman, because she was misled by the owner's failure to complain when the woman was building her house.
C. the owner if, but only if, it can be shown that the owner's intention to erect such a building was made known to the woman at or prior to the time of the owner's conveyance to her.
D. the owner, because the woman has no easement for light, air, or view.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Property rights, specifically the absence of inherent rights to sunlight, fresh air, or view, and the concept of easements.

Fact Analysis: The woman built a house on her lot with a large window providing a view, which added value to her property. The owner retained a neighboring lot and later decided to build an apartment house that would block the woman's view. The woman seeks to enjoin the owner from erecting the building.

Rule Application: A landowner has rights to their property and the areas above and below it, but there are no inherent rights to sunlight, fresh air, or view. The woman does not have a natural right to an easement for light and air, and her reliance on the owner's failure to complain during her construction is irrelevant. The owner's intention to erect the building is also irrelevant to determining the woman's rights.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the woman has no legal basis for a cause of action against the owner due to the absence of inherent rights to sunlight, fresh air, or view, the decision should be for the owner. The woman does not possess an easement for light, air, or view, supporting option D.

Five years ago, a woman acquired Blackacre, improved with a 15-year-old dwelling. This year the woman listed Blackacre for sale with a licensed real estate broker. The woman informed the broker of several defects in the house that were not readily discoverable by a reasonable inspection, including a leaky basement, an inadequate water supply, and a roof that leaked. The plaintiff responded to the broker's advertisement, was taken by the broker to view Blackacre, and decided to buy it. The broker saw to it that the contract specified the property to be "as is" but neither the broker nor the woman pointed out the defects to the plaintiff, who did not ask about the condition of the dwelling. After closing and taking possession, the plaintiff discovered the defects, had them repaired, and demanded that the woman reimburse him for the cost of the repairs. The woman refused and the plaintiff brought an appropriate action against the woman for damages. If the woman wins, it will be because

Choices:
A. the woman fulfilled the duty to disclose defects by disclosure to the broker.
B. the contract's "as is" provision controls the rights of the parties.
C. the broker became the agent of both the plaintiff and the woman and thus knowledge of the defects was imputed to the plaintiff.
D. the seller of a used dwelling that has been viewed by the buyer has no responsibility toward the buyer.

Answer: B

Legal Concept: Disclosure of defects in real property transactions, specifically the seller's obligations and the effect of 'as is' provisions.

Fact Analysis: The woman listed her property, Blackacre, for sale through a broker, informing the broker of several non-obvious defects. The plaintiff viewed the property and agreed to purchase it 'as is' without being directly informed of the defects by the woman or the broker.

Rule Application: Sellers are generally required to disclose known defects that are not open and obvious to buyers. However, an 'as is' provision in a contract may suffice to put the buyer on notice of potential defects, potentially limiting the seller's liability for undisclosed defects.

Legal Conclusion: Given the 'as is' provision in the contract, the woman may not be liable for the defects, as this provision could be seen as sufficient notice to the plaintiff of potential issues with the property. Therefore, the correct answer is B, as the 'as is' provision controls the rights of the parties.

Blackacre was a tract of 100 acres retained by the owner after he had developed the adjoining 400 acres as a residential subdivision. The owner had effectively imposed restrictive covenants on each lot in the 400 acres. A buyer offered the owner a good price for a five-acre tract located in a corner of Blackacre far away from the existing 400-acre residential subdivision. The owner conveyed the five-acre tract to the buyer and imposed the same restrictive covenants on the five-acre tract as he had imposed on the lots in the adjoining 400 acres. The owner further covenanted that when he sold the remaining 95 acres of Blackacre he would impose the same restrictive convenants in the deed or deeds for the 95 acres. The owner's conveyance to the buyer was promptly and properly recorded. However, shortly thereafter, the owner conveyed the remaining 95 acres to a businessman for $100,000 by a deed that made no mention of any restrictive convenants in the buyer's deed. The businessman now proposes to build an industrial park which would violate such restrictive covenants if they are applicable. The recording act of the jurisdiction provides: "No conveyance or mortgage of real property shall be good against subsequent purchasers for value and without notice unless the same be recorded according to law." In an appropriate action by the buyer to enforce the restrictive covenants against the businessman's 95-acre tract, if the businessman wins it will be because

Choices:
A. the deed imposing the restrictions was not in the chain of title for the 95 acres when the businessman bought them.
B. the disparity in acreage means that the covenant can only be personal to the owner.
C. negative reciprocal covenants are not generally recognized.
D. a covenant to impose restrictions is an illegal restraint on alienation.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: The enforceability of restrictive covenants against subsequent purchasers of real property under a notice-type recording act.

Fact Analysis: The owner conveyed a five-acre tract of Blackacre to the buyer with restrictive covenants and promised to include the same covenants in future sales of the remaining 95 acres. However, when the owner sold the 95 acres to the businessman, the deed did not mention the restrictive covenants. The businessman was not aware of the covenants and proposes to build an industrial park, which would violate them.

Rule Application: Under a notice-type recording act, a subsequent purchaser is protected from earlier purchasers if they recorded their deed without notice of the earlier purchasers. In this case, a title search on the 95 acres would not have revealed any deeds including the residential subdivision restrictions. The businessman purchased the land without notice of the restrictive covenants, so they cannot be enforced against him.

Legal Conclusion: The businessman will prevail because the deed imposing the restrictions was not in the chain of title for the 95 acres when he bought them, making him a bona fide purchaser without notice. Therefore, the correct answer is A.

Several years ago, a carpenter purchased Goldacre, financing a large part of the purchase price by a loan from a bank that was secured by a mortgage. The carpenter made the installment payments on the mortgage regularly until last year. Then the carpenter persuaded a friend to buy Goldacre, subject to the mortgage to the bank. They expressly agreed that the friend would not assume and agree to pay the carpenter's debt to the bank. The carpenter's mortgage to the bank contained a due-on-sale clause stating, "If Mortgagor transfers his/her interest without the written consent of Mortgagee first obtained, then at Mortgagee's option the entire principal balance of the debt secured by this Mortgage shall become immediately due and payable." However, without seeking the bank's consent, the carpenter conveyed Goldacre to the friend, the deed stating in pertinent part ". . . subject to a mortgage to the bank [giving details and recording data]." The friend took possession of Goldacre and made several mortgage payments, which the bank accepted. Now, however, neither the friend nor the carpenter has made the last three mortgage payments. The bank has brought an appropriate action against the friend for the amount of the delinquent payments. In this action, judgment should be for

Choices:
A. the friend, because she did not assume and agree to pay the carpenter's mortgage debt.
B. the friend, because she is not in privity of estate with the bank.
C. the bank, because the carpenter's deed to the friend violated the due-on-sale clause.
D. the bank, because the friend is in privity of estate with the bank.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Mortgage law, specifically the concept of assumption of mortgage debt and the effect of a due-on-sale clause.

Fact Analysis: The carpenter conveyed Goldacre to the friend subject to the mortgage, without the bank's consent, and the friend did not assume the mortgage debt. The friend made several mortgage payments, which the bank accepted, but later stopped making payments.

Rule Application: A grantee who does not assume a mortgage debt is not personally liable for the debt, but the property remains subject to the mortgage. The due-on-sale clause allows the bank to demand immediate payment of the entire outstanding mortgage balance if the property is transferred without the bank's consent.

Legal Conclusion: Since the friend did not assume the mortgage debt, she is not personally liable for the delinquent payments. The bank's action against the friend for the amount of the delinquent payments should be dismissed, supporting option A.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Mortgage assumption and the resulting liability for deficiency judgments in the context of real property transactions.

Fact Analysis: The buyer agreed to assume the existing mortgage debt on the residence as part of the contract of sale. Following the buyer's default on the mortgage loan, foreclosure proceedings resulted in a deficiency.

Rule Application: When a buyer assumes a mortgage, they become primarily liable for the mortgage debt and any deficiency that may arise from foreclosure proceedings. In contrast, if the property were purchased 'subject to the mortgage,' only the original debtor would be liable for any deficiency.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the buyer assumed the mortgage debt, the buyer is primarily liable for the deficiency resulting from the foreclosure sale. Therefore, the correct answer is that the buyer is liable for the deficiency, supporting option C.

A niece inherited vacant land from her uncle. She lived in a distant state and decided to sell the land to a colleague who was interested in purchasing the land as an investment. They orally agreed upon a price, and, at the colleague's insistence, the niece agreed to provide him with a warranty deed without any exceptions. The price was paid, the warranty deed was delivered, and the deed was promptly and properly recorded. Neither the niece nor the colleague had, at that point, ever seen the land. After recording the deed, the colleague visited the land for the first time and discovered that it had no access to any public right-of-way and that none of the surrounding lands had ever been held in common ownership with any previous owner of the tract of land. The colleague sued the niece for damages. For whom will the court find?

Choices:
A. The colleague, because lack of access makes title unmarketable.
B. The colleague, because the covenants of warranty and quiet enjoyment in the deed were breached.
C. The niece, because no title covenants were breached.
D. The niece, because the agreement to sell was oral.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: The concept of marketable title in real estate law, specifically the timing and implications of challenging title defects.

Fact Analysis: The niece and colleague entered into an oral agreement for the sale of vacant land, with the colleague insisting on a warranty deed without exceptions. The deed was delivered and recorded, but upon visiting the land, the colleague discovered it had no access to a public right-of-way.

Rule Application: A challenge to marketable title must be made prior to the acceptance of the deed. Once the deed is accepted, the contract of sale is complete, and any title defects are deemed waived. The covenants of warranty and quiet enjoyment in the deed do not guarantee access to a public right-of-way.

Legal Conclusion: Since the colleague accepted the deed, thereby completing the contract of sale, the lack of access does not render the title unmarketable, and no title covenants were breached. Therefore, the court will find for the niece, supporting option C.

A well-known politician was scheduled to address a large crowd at a political dinner. Just as he was about to sit down at the head table, the defendant pushed the politician's chair to one side. As a result, the politician fell to the floor. The politician was embarrassed at being made to look foolish before a large audience but suffered no physical harm. Assume that the defendant knew that the politician was about to sit in the chair before he pushed it. If the politician asserts a claim against the defendant for damages because of his embarrassment, will the politician prevail?

Choices:
A. Yes, because the defendant knew that the politician was about to sit on the chair.
B. Yes, because the defendant negligently failed to notice that the politician would fall.
C. No, because the politician suffered no physical harm along with his embarrassment.
D. No, because the defendant intended moving the chair to be a good-natured practical joke on the politician.

Answer: A

Legal Concept: Battery as a dignitary tort, specifically the elements required for a claim of battery including the unlawful application of force resulting in offensive touching without consent or privilege.

Fact Analysis: The defendant pushed a chair knowing the politician was about to sit on it, causing the politician to fall to the floor without suffering physical harm but experiencing embarrassment.

Rule Application: Battery is a general intent crime that does not require direct application of force. The defendant's action of pushing the chair with knowledge that the politician was about to sit on it constitutes an offensive touching, fulfilling the elements of battery. The fact that the defendant intended it as a good-natured practical joke does not negate the battery, as only general intent is required.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the defendant committed a battery by causing an offensive touching without consent or privilege, the politician can recover for the harm to his dignity, supporting option A.

A farmer kept antiques in an uninhabited farmhouse on his property. The farmhouse had been broken into several times in the past, and some of the farmer's goods had been stolen. Instead of posting "No Trespassing" signs, the farmer decided to install an alarm system to deter intruders. While the farmer was in the farmhouse installing the alarm system, he heard a window open in the adjoining room. The farmer crept very quietly to the door of the room, threw the door open, and found an intruder, a young child. The farmer immediately struck the child, a 10-year-old girl, very hard in the face, breaking her nose. In an action on behalf of the child against the farmer to recover for the injury to her nose, is the child likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No, because the farmer did not use deadly force.
B. No, because the farmer had probable cause to believe that the child was a thief.
C. Yes, because the farmer should have posted a "No Trespassing" sign.
D. Yes, because the farmer used excessive force.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: The privilege to use reasonable force to protect one's property, and the limits of such privilege when the force used threatens serious bodily injury.

Fact Analysis: The farmer, while installing an alarm system in his uninhabited farmhouse, discovered a 10-year-old girl intruder. Instead of using less forceful means to deter her, the farmer struck the child very hard in the face, breaking her nose. The child posed no threat of bodily harm to the farmer.

Rule Application: A property owner is privileged to use reasonable force to prevent or end a trespasser's intrusion or to protect property, but not to use force that threatens serious bodily injury unless in danger of serious bodily harm themselves. The force used must be proportionate to the threat posed.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the farmer used excessive force against the child, who posed no threat of bodily harm, the child is likely to prevail in her action against the farmer. The force used was not only unnecessary but also intended to cause serious bodily harm, making it excessive as a defense of property.

A real estate developer was trying to purchase land on which he intended to build a large commercial development. An elderly widow had rejected all of the developer's offers to buy her ancestral home, where she had lived all her life and which was located in the middle of the developer's planned development. Finally, the developer offered her $250,000. He told her that if she rejected it, state law authorized him to have her property condemned. He subsequently parked a bulldozer in front of her house. The widow then consulted her nephew, a law student, who researched the question and advised her that the developer had no power of condemnation under state law. The widow had been badly frightened by the developer's threat, and was outraged when she learned that the developer had lied to her. If the widow sues the developer for damages for emotional distress, will she prevail?

Choices:
A. Yes, because the developer's action was extreme and outrageous.
B. Yes, because the widow was frightened and outraged.
C. No, because the widow did not suffer emotional distress that was severe.
D. No, because it was not the developer's purpose to cause emotional distress.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Intentional infliction of emotional distress (IIED), specifically the elements required to establish a claim for IIED.

Fact Analysis: The developer made an extreme and outrageous threat to the widow, stating he could have her property condemned under state law if she didn't sell, and then parked a bulldozer in front of her house. The widow was frightened and outraged upon learning the developer had lied about his power of condemnation.

Rule Application: To succeed in a claim for IIED, a plaintiff must show: (1) the defendant's intentional or reckless conduct was extreme and outrageous, (2) the conduct caused the plaintiff severe emotional distress. While the developer's actions were extreme and outrageous, and he acted with the knowledge to a substantial certainty that the widow would be frightened, the key issue is whether the widow suffered severe emotional distress.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the facts only indicate the widow was 'frightened' and 'outraged' without specifying severe emotional distress, the widow's claim for IIED would not prevail due to insufficient evidence of severe emotional distress, supporting option C.

A rancher and his neighbor were involved in a boundary dispute. In order to resolve their differences, each drove his truck to an open pasture area on his land where the two properties were separated by a fence. The rancher was accompanied by four friends, and the neighbor was alone. The neighbor got out of his truck and walked toward the fence. The rancher got out but simply stood by his truck. When the neighbor came over the fence, the rancher shot him, inflicting serious injury. In a battery action brought by the neighbor against the rancher, the rancher testified that he actually thought his neighbor was armed, although he could point to nothing that would have reasonably justified this belief. Is the neighbor likely to prevail?

Choices:
A. No, because the rancher was standing on his own property and had no obligation to retreat.
B. No, because the rancher suspected that the neighbor was armed.
C. Yes, because deadly force is never appropriate in a property dispute.
D. Yes, because it was unreasonable for the rancher to consider the use of a gun necessary for self-defense.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: The use of deadly force in self-defense, particularly the requirement of a reasonable belief of imminent harm.

Fact Analysis: The rancher and his neighbor were involved in a boundary dispute, leading to a confrontation where the neighbor crossed the fence and the rancher shot him, claiming he believed the neighbor was armed, despite no evidence supporting this belief.

Rule Application: To justify the use of force sufficient to cause death or serious bodily injury, a defendant must have an actual and reasonable belief that he himself is threatened with force of that sort. The use of deadly force is not justified by a mere subjective suspicion, but rather requires a reasonable belief of imminent harm.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the rancher's belief that the neighbor was armed was not reasonable and he had no evidence to support his claim of fearing imminent harm, his use of deadly force was unjustified. Therefore, the neighbor is likely to prevail in a battery action, supporting option D.

A plaintiff sustained personal injuries in a three-car collision caused by the concurrent negligence of all three drivers. In the plaintiff's action for damages against the other two drivers, the jury apportioned the negligence 30% to the plaintiff, 30% to driver #1, and 40% to driver #2. The plaintiff's total damages were $100,000. Assume that the state has retained the common-law rule pertaining to contribution and that the state's comparative negligence statute provides for a system of pure comparative negligence but abolishes joint and several liability. If the plaintiff chooses to pursue the claim against driver #1 alone, she will be entitled to collect at most

Choices:
A. $70,000 from driver #1, and then driver #1 will be entitled to collect $40,000 from driver #2.
B. $30,000 from driver #1, and then driver #1 will be entitled to collect $10,000 from driver #2.
C. $30,000 from driver #1, and then driver #1 will be entitled to collect nothing from driver #2.
D. nothing from driver #1, because his percentage of fault is not greater than that of the plaintiff.

Answer: C

Legal Concept: Comparative negligence and the abolition of joint and several liability in tort law, specifically the implications for damages recovery and contribution between defendants.

Fact Analysis: A three-car collision occurred due to the concurrent negligence of all three drivers, with the plaintiff's damages totaling $100,000. The jury apportioned negligence as 30% to the plaintiff, 30% to driver #1, and 40% to driver #2. The state has abolished joint and several liability and follows a pure comparative negligence system.

Rule Application: In a pure comparative negligence system without joint and several liability, each defendant is liable only for their proportionate share of the damages. Contribution between defendants is only available if one defendant pays more than their determined share. The plaintiff can recover damages minus their percentage of fault, but defendants are not jointly and severally liable.

Legal Conclusion: Given the abolition of joint and several liability and the principles of pure comparative negligence, the plaintiff can recover $30,000 from driver #1, who is liable only for his share of the damages. Driver #1 is not entitled to collect from driver #2 because he has not paid more than his determined share of liability, and contribution is not available.

A property owner owns a hotel. When the International Order of Badgers came to town for its convention, its members rented 400 of the 500 rooms, and the hotel opened its convention facilities to them. During their convention, the members littered both the inside and the outside of the hotel with debris and bottles. The hotel manager knew that objects were being thrown out of the hotel windows. At his direction, hotel employees patrolled the hallways telling the guests to refrain from such conduct. The owner was out of town and was not aware of the problems which were occurring. During the convention, as a pedestrian walked past the hotel on the sidewalk, he was hit and injured by an ashtray thrown out of a window in the hotel by an unknown person. The pedestrian sued the owner for damages for his injuries. Will the pedestrian prevail in his claim against the owner?

Choices:
A. Yes, because a property owner is strictly liable for acts on his premises if such acts cause harm to persons using the adjacent public sidewalks.
B. Yes, because the person who threw the ashtray cannot be identified.
C. No, because the owner had no personal knowledge of the conduct of the hotel guests.
D. No, because the hotel employees had taken reasonable precautions to prevent such an injury.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Premises liability, specifically the duty of care owed by a property owner to licensees and the standard of care required in conducting active operations.

Fact Analysis: The hotel owner rented rooms to the International Order of Badgers for their convention, and despite knowing about the guests' misconduct, the hotel manager took steps to prevent harm by having employees patrol the hallways and warn guests. However, an unknown guest threw an ashtray out of the window, injuring a pedestrian on the sidewalk.

Rule Application: A property owner owes a duty of reasonable care to licensees, such as pedestrians passing by the property. This duty includes taking reasonable precautions to prevent harm from active operations. The owner is not strictly liable for harm caused by active operations unless the activity is ultra-hazardous, which hosting a convention is not. The fact that the hotel employees took reasonable precautions against injury to passersby means the owner has not breached his duty of care.

Legal Conclusion: Given that the hotel employees took reasonable precautions to prevent harm, the owner will not be found liable for the pedestrian's injury. Therefore, the correct answer is D, as the owner is not liable due to the reasonable precautions taken by the hotel employees.

A plaintiff's three-year-old daughter was killed in an automobile accident. At the plaintiff's direction, the child's body was taken to a mausoleum for interment. The owner of a truck leasing company asked one of his employees to deliver $1,000 to the dealership's main office. The following week, as a result of a dispute over whether the money had been delivered, the owner instructed the employee to come to the office to submit to a lie detector test. When the employee reported to the owner's office for the test, it was not administered. Instead, without hearing the employee's story, the owner shouted at him, "You're a thief!" and fired him. At the time the owner accused the employee of stealing, the owner believed the charge to be true. The owner's shout was overheard by several other employees who were in another office that was separated from the owner's office by a thin partition. The next day, the employee accepted another job at a higher salary. Several weeks later, upon discovering that the money had not been stolen, the owner offered to rehire the employee. In a suit for slander by the employee against the owner, the employee will

Choices:
A. prevail, because the employee was fraudulently induced to go to the office for a lie detector test, which was not, in fact, given.
B. prevail, because the owner should have foreseen that the statement would be overheard by other employees.
C. not prevail, because the owner made the charge in good faith, believing it to be true.
D. not prevail, because the statement was made to the employee alone and intended for his ears only.

Answer: B

Fact Analysis: The owner of a truck leasing company accused an employee of theft in the presence of other employees, despite believing the charge to be true at the time. A customer ordered some merchandise from a store. When the merchandise was delivered, the customer decided that it was not what he had ordered, and he returned it for credit. The store refused to credit the customer's account, continued to bill him, and, after 90 days, turned the account over to a bill collector for collection. The bill collector showed up at the customer's house at 7 p.m. on a summer evening while many of the customer's neighbors were seated on their porches. When the customer opened the door, the bill collector, who was standing just outside the door, raised an electrically amplified bullhorn to his mouth. In a voice that could be heard a block away, the bill collector called the customer a "deadbeat" and asked him when he intended to pay his bill to the store. The customer, greatly angered, slammed the door shut. The door struck the bullhorn and jammed it forcibly against the bill collector's face. As a consequence, the bill collector lost some of his front teeth. If the customer asserts a claim based on defamation against the bill collector, will the customer prevail?

Choices:
A. Yes, because the bill collector's remarks were heard by the customer's neighbors.
B. Yes, because the bill collector's conduct was extreme and outrageous.
C. No, because the bill collector did not know that the customer owed no money to the store.
D. No, because the customer did not suffer any special damages.

Answer: D

Legal Concept: Defamation, specifically the elements required to prove a claim of slander (verbal defamation) and the exceptions that do not require special damages.

Fact Analysis: The bill collector verbally called the customer a 'deadbeat' using an amplified bullhorn in front of the customer's neighbors, but the customer did not suffer any pecuniary damages as a result of the statement.

Rule Application: To prevail in a defamation claim for slander, the plaintiff must prove a defamatory communication of fact, publication to a third person who understood it as defamatory, and resulting harm. Special damages are required unless the statement falls under one of four exceptions: allegations of criminal activity, occupational misconduct, sexual misconduct, or having a 'loathsome' disease.

Legal Conclusion: Since the bill collector's statement does not fit into any of the exceptions and the customer did not suffer special damages, the customer will not prevail in his defamation claim against the bill collector.
